proofs.proof_tex:
We prove the narrowed statement at \(s=1\).  In this case
\[
 H=\frac{\kappa_n}{2^{12}M},\qquad
 b=m^{-1/3},\qquad
 T_n=n\kappa_n^3,\qquad
 \rho_n=n^{-1/3}.
 \tag{8}
\]
Put
\[
 L_\alpha=\log(32/\alpha),\qquad
 A_\alpha=2^{16}L_\alpha,
\]
\[
 B_{M,\alpha}
 =1+\log\!\left(\frac{16(1+2^{17}M)}{\alpha}\right),
\]
and define the following finite constants:
\[
 C_r
 =8M+16A_\alpha+1+16M(A_\alpha+1)+8\sqrt{L_\alpha},
\]
\[
 c_3=2^{-24}M^{-1},\qquad c_2=2^{-22},
\]
\[
 C_F
 =2(3e c_3)^{-1/3}+12(2e c_2)^{-1/2},
 \qquad
 C_2=16C_r+4C_F,
\]
and
\[
 C_1=\max\left\{
 2^{27}MB_{M,\alpha},\;
 2^{15}M(8A_\alpha+1),\;
 8(8C_r)^3,\;
 2^{30}ML_\alpha
 \right\}.
 \tag{9}
\]
These displayed choices are not optimized; their role is to make every
deterministic and probability inequality below simultaneous.

For sufficiently large \(n\), \(m\ge n/8\).  Since
\(N_H\le1+2^{17}M/\kappa_n\),
\[
 \log(16N_H/\alpha)
 \le B_{M,\alpha}\log(e/\kappa_n).
 \tag{10}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 2^{-11}mH\kappa_n^2
 \ge\frac{T_n}{2^{26}M}.
 \tag{11}
\]
Thus the first term in (9), the signal condition, and the localization
lemma imply
\[
 P(\mathcal E_1^c)\le\alpha/8.
 \tag{12}
\]
The same lemma, with
\(R_c=A_\alpha/(m\kappa_n^2)+1/n\), gives
\[
 P\bigl(\{|\widehat c-c_P|>R_c\}\cap\mathcal E_1\bigr)
 \le9e^{-L_\alpha}=\frac{9\alpha}{32}.
 \tag{13}
\]
Here \(R_c\ge16/n\), because \(m\le n/4\),
\(\kappa_n\le1/8\), and \(A_\alpha>1\).

We next check the two deterministic fallbacks.  Let
\(q=\kappa_n/b\).  Since \(b^{-3}=m\) and \(m\ge n/8\),
\[
 q^3=m\kappa_n^3\ge T_n/8.
 \tag{14}
\]
For \(q\ge1\), direct substitution into the definition of \(r_n\)
and \(1/n\le1/(4m)=b^3/4\) yields
\[
 r_n
 \le C_rb.
 \tag{15}
\]
Indeed, the four terms, divided by \(b\), are bounded respectively by
\(8M\), \(16A_\alpha+1\), \(16M(A_\alpha+1)\), and
\(8\sqrt{L_\alpha}\).  Equations (9), (14), and (15) give
\(r_n\le\kappa_n/8\).  Also
\[
 \frac{R_c}{H}
 =2^{12}M\left\{
 \frac{A_\alpha}{m\kappa_n^3}+\frac{1}{n\kappa_n}
 \right\}
 \le\frac{2^{12}M(8A_\alpha+1)}{T_n}
 \le\frac18,
 \tag{16}
\]
where \(n\kappa_n\ge n\kappa_n^3=T_n\).  Thus the signal condition
forces both deterministic checks in the definition to pass.

We now prove honesty.  Fix \(P\in\mathcal P_n\), and abbreviate
\(\theta=\theta_P\).  The identifying proposition and binary potential
outcomes imply \(|\theta|\le1\) and
\(y_P-\theta d_P=0\).  Consequently the conditional regression of
\(U=Y-\theta D\), separately on the two sides of \(c_P\), is
\(2M\)-Lipschitz and has zero level jump.  Gluing the two pieces at
their common value makes it globally \(2M\)-Lipschitz.  Conditional on
folds one through three, \(\widehat c\) is fixed and fold four remains
independent by \(\textnormal{ass:iid-sampling}\).  On
\(|\widehat c-c_P|\le R_c\), therefore,
\[
 \left|E_P\left[
 \widehat y(\widehat c)-\theta\widehat d(\widehat c)
 \mid F_1,F_2,F_3\right]\right|
 \le2Mb.
 \tag{17}
\]
For treatment, (1)--(3), now at bandwidth \(b\), give
\[
 \left|E_P[\widehat d(\widehat c)\mid F_1,F_2,F_3]-d_P\right|
 \le Mb+\frac{2\kappa_nR_c}{b}+2MR_c.
 \tag{18}
\]
All divisions in (18) are legitimate because \(b>0\).  Moreover, the
nonnegative term \(16\kappa_nR_c/b\) in \(r_n\), together with
\(r_n\le\kappa_n/8\), gives \(R_c/b\le1/128\), so the shift lies inside
the kernel window.

The fold-four summands are bounded and are nonzero only on a set of
\(X\)-probability \(2b\).  Here \(|U|\le2\), so the conditional second
moment is at most \(8\|K_0\|_\infty^2/b\) for \(U\), and it is at most
\(2\|K_0\|_\infty^2/b\) for \(D\).  Applying the same exponential
calculation as in (5), conditionally on the first three folds, gives
\[
 \left|\widehat\Delta_{4,b}^{U}(\widehat c)
       -E_P[\widehat\Delta_{4,b}^{U}(\widehat c)\mid F_1,F_2,F_3]
 \right|
 \le8\|K_0\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{L_\alpha}{mb}},
 \tag{19}
\]
and the analogous inequality with constant four for \(D\), except on
an event of probability at most \(\alpha/8\).  The linear Bernstein term
is absorbed by the displayed square-root terms for all sufficiently
large \(n\), because \(mb\to\infty\).  Combining (17)--(19) with the
definition of \(r_n\) shows
\[
 \left|\widehat y(\widehat c)-
       \theta_P\widehat d(\widehat c)\right|\le2r_n.
 \tag{20}
\]
If the empirical denominator is below \(\kappa_n/2\), the rule returns
\(\Theta\), which contains \(\theta_P\); otherwise (20) puts
\(\theta_P\) in the inverted set.  By (12), (13), and (19), the failure
probability is at most
\[
 \frac\alpha8+\frac{9\alpha}{32}+\frac\alpha8
 =\frac{17\alpha}{32}<\alpha.
\]
The bound does not depend on \(P\), proving uniform honesty.

It remains to control expected length rather than only coverage.  If
\(\widehat d(\widehat c)\ge\kappa_n/2\), the accepted labels form an
interval of length at most
\[
 \frac{4r_n}{\widehat d(\widehat c)}
 \le\frac{8r_n}{\kappa_n}.
 \tag{21}
\]
On the event \(|\widehat c-c_P|\le b/8\), (18), the inequality
\(Mb\le r_n/8\le\kappa_n/64\), and a fold-four treatment fluctuation
of at most \(\kappa_n/8\) imply
\(\widehat d(\widehat c)>\kappa_n/2\).  Hence the full-length fallback
event is contained in a coarse-scan failure, a localization error larger
than \(b/8\), or a fold-four deviation larger than \(\kappa_n/8\).
Equations (5), (10)--(14), and the localization lemma consequently give
\[
 P\{\widehat d(\widehat c)<\kappa_n/2\}
 \le2e^{-c_3q^3}+12e^{-c_2q^2}.
 \tag{22}
\]
The elementary optimizations
\[
 \sup_{q\ge1}q e^{-c_3q^3}\le(3ec_3)^{-1/3},
 \qquad
 \sup_{q\ge1}q e^{-c_2q^2}\le(2ec_2)^{-1/2}
\]
turn (22) into
\[
 P\{\widehat d(\widehat c)<\kappa_n/2\}
 \le C_F\frac{b}{\kappa_n}.
 \tag{23}
\]
Since \(m\ge n/8\), \(b\le2\rho_n\).  Taking expectations in (21),
using length at most two on the fallback, and applying (15) and (23),
gives
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P|I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}|
 \le\frac{8C_rb}{\kappa_n}
      +\frac{2C_Fb}{\kappa_n}
 \le C_2\frac{\rho_n}{\kappa_n}.
 \tag{24}
\]
By (14) and (9), \(\rho_n/\kappa_n<1\) in the asserted region, so the
right side of (24) is exactly of the claimed
\(\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}\) order.

Finally, every unknown-cutoff interval rule induces a known-cutoff rule
that ignores the supplied \(c_P\).  Therefore
\(L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\le L_n(\kappa_n)\).  The already proved
known-cutoff benchmark and (24) imply
\[
 c_0\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}
 \le L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)
 \le L_n(\kappa_n)
 \le C_2\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}.
\]
This proves oracle-order attainment and completes the proof.

added_lemmas.statement:
Suppose \(s=1\), \(P\in\mathcal P_n\), and use the notation in the
definition of \(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}\).  Write
\(\Delta_H^D(t)=E_P[\widehat\Delta_{j,H}^D(t)]\), which is independent
of \(j\), and define
\[
 \mathcal E_1=\left\{
 \max_{t\in\mathcal G_H}
 \left|\widehat\Delta_{1,H}^{D}(t)-\Delta_H^D(t)\right|
 \le\frac{\kappa_n}{16}\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
 P(\mathcal E_1^c)
 \le2N_H\exp\{-2^{-11}mH\kappa_n^2\},
 \qquad N_H\le1+32/H,
\]
every retained \(H\)-neighborhood is contained in
\([c_P-2H,c_P+2H]\) on \(\mathcal E_1\), and, for every
\(u\ge16/n\),
\[
 P\bigl(\{|\widehat c-c_P|>u\}\cap\mathcal E_1\bigr)
 \le9\exp\{-2^{-16}m\kappa_n^2u\}.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Put \(f(x)=E_P[D\mid X=x]\).  By
\(\textnormal{ass:observable-holder-extensions}\) at \(s=1\), the two
one-sided extensions are \(M\)-Lipschitz.  Let
\(a=f(c_P-)\), \(d=f(c_P+)-f(c_P-)=d_P\), and define
\[
 e(x)=
 \begin{cases}
 f(x)-a,&x<c_P,\\
 f(x)-a-d,&x\ge c_P.
 \end{cases}
\]
The two pieces vanish at \(c_P\).  Hence each is \(M\)-Lipschitz on
its side, and, if \(x<c_P<y\),
\(|e(y)-e(x)|\le M(y-c_P)+M(c_P-x)=M(y-x)\).  Thus \(e\) is globally
\(M\)-Lipschitz and
\[
 f(x)=a+d\mathbf 1\{x\ge c_P\}+e(x).
 \tag{1}
\]
Uniformity of \(X\), from
\(\textnormal{ass:uniform-running-variable}\), and the moment
\(\int_0^1K_0=1\) give
\[
 \Delta_H^D(t)
 =d\left(1-\frac{|t-c_P|}{H}\right)_++Q_e(t),
 \qquad
 Q_e(t)=\frac1H\int_0^H\{e(t+x)-e(t-x)\}\,dx.
 \tag{2}
\]
The Lipschitz property yields
\[
 |Q_e(t)|\le MH,
 \qquad
 |Q_e(t)-Q_e(q)|\le2M|t-q|.
 \tag{3}
\]
There is a point \(q\in\mathcal G_H\) with
\(|q-c_P|\le H/64\), including at the trimmed endpoints.  Since
\(d\ge\kappa_n\) by
\(\textnormal{ass:local-compliance-strength}\) and
\(MH=\kappa_n/2^{12}\), (2)--(3) imply
\[
 \Delta_H^D(q)
 \ge\frac{63}{64}\kappa_n-\frac{\kappa_n}{2^{12}},
 \qquad
 \sup_{|t-c_P|\ge H}|\Delta_H^D(t)|
 \le\frac{\kappa_n}{2^{12}}.
 \tag{4}
\]

For fixed \(t\), one summand in
\(\widehat\Delta_{1,H}^D(t)\) has absolute value at most \(H^{-1}\)
and second moment at most \(2H^{-1}\).  Its centered version is bounded
by \(2H^{-1}\).  The elementary Bernstein calculation
\[
 P\{|m^{-1}\textstyle\sum_{i\in F_1}(W_i-EW_i)|>x\}
 \le2\exp\left\{-\frac{mx^2}{4/H+4x/(3H)}\right\}
 \tag{5}
\]
follows from independence in \(\textnormal{ass:iid-sampling}\) and
\(e^z\le1+z+z^2/[2(1-|z|/3)]\) for \(|z|<3\).  At
\(x=\kappa_n/16\le1\), (5) is at most
\(2\exp\{-2^{-11}mH\kappa_n^2\}\).  The union bound over
\(N_H\) grid points proves the first display of the lemma.  On
\(\mathcal E_1\), (4) and two deviations of size
\(\kappa_n/16\) show that no point at distance at least \(H\) can be
within \(\kappa_n/8\) of the empirical maximum.  Thus every retained
center is within \(H\) of \(c_P\), proving the asserted containment of
their \(H\)-neighborhoods.

It remains to control the local maximizer.  From (2)--(3), for
\(|t-c_P|\le H\),
\[
 \Delta_H^D(c_P)-\Delta_H^D(t)
 \ge\left(\frac{\kappa_n}{H}-2M\right)|t-c_P|
 \ge\frac{\kappa_n}{2H}|t-c_P|,
 \tag{6}
\]
where the last inequality uses \(H=\kappa_n/(2^{12}M)\).  For
\(H\le|t-c_P|\le2H\), the same equations give a loss at least
\(\kappa_n/2\).  Let \(c_n\) be a point of
\(\mathcal G_n(\mathcal A_H)\) within \(1/n\) of \(c_P\).  The
Lipschitz constant of the right side of (2) is at most
\(2\kappa_n/H+2M\), so, whenever \(u\ge16/n\), the grid error is
absorbed by one quarter of the lower bound in (6).

For completeness, the maximal calculation needed here is obtained
directly from (5), without a union bound over the \(1/n\) mesh.  For
\(t>c_n\), the difference between the two kernel weights is supported
on the three moving boundary strips at \(c_n-H,c_n,c_n+H\); the middle
strip has coefficient two and the other two have coefficient one.
Up to distance \(r\), its squared weight therefore integrates to at
most \(6r/H^2\), and its absolute weight is at most \(2/H\).  Reveal
the observations in each strip in increasing \(X\)-order.  Applying
the exponential bound used in (5) at the first crossing of the line
\(\kappa_n r/(8H)\) gives, on the dyadic block
\(2^ju\le r<2^{j+1}u\),
\[
 P\left\{
 \sup_{2^ju\le t-c_n<2^{j+1}u}
 \bigl[(\overline\Delta_H^D-E\overline\Delta_H^D)(t)
 -(\overline\Delta_H^D-E\overline\Delta_H^D)(c_n)\bigr]
 \ge\frac{\kappa_n2^ju}{8H}
 \right\}
 \le2e^{-2^{-13}m\kappa_n^2 2^ju}.
 \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, the product conditional moment-generating function before the
first crossing is bounded by
\(\exp\{12m\lambda^2(2^{j+1}u)/H^2\}\); choosing
\(\lambda=\kappa_nH/2^7\), and using \(\kappa_n\le1/8\), gives (7).
The same argument in decreasing \(X\)-order handles \(t<c_n\).
Summing the two geometric series in \(j\), and using (6) outside the
first block, gives
\[
 P\bigl(\{|\widehat c-c_P|>u\}\cap\mathcal E_1\bigr)
 \le9e^{-2^{-16}m\kappa_n^2u}.
\]
For \(u>2H\) the event on the left is empty by the containment already
proved.  This establishes the claimed bound for every \(u\ge16/n\).

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
Suppose \(s=1\).  There are constants \(C_1,C_2<\infty\), depending
only on \(M,v,\alpha\), such that, for all sufficiently large \(n\), if
\(T_n\ge C_1\log(e/\kappa_n)\), then the sample map
\(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}\) is uniformly honest over \(\mathcal P_n\) and
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P[|I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}|]
 \le C_2\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}.
\]
Consequently \(L_n(\kappa_n)\asymp
L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\) in this region, uniformly over
vanishing \(\kappa_n\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason:
For \(s>1\), the requested scan is not uniformly centered at \(c_P\)
under the frozen observable-smoothness class.  To see the obstruction,
take \(c_P=1/2\), let the left treatment regression be constant, and let
the right treatment regression have jump \(d_P=\kappa_n\) and a fixed
positive slope \(\gamma\le\min\{M/16,1/8\}\).  These observable
regressions have radius at most \(M\); monotone potential treatment
means can realize them with constant complier probability \(\kappa_n\),
because the unobserved side of each potential-treatment regression is
only required to be continuous.  With common independent fair binary
potential outcomes, the outcome-variance and correlation conditions
also hold.  For \(K_1(u)=4-6u\), direct integration gives, for
\(0\le z\le1\),
\[
 E_P\widehat\Delta_{j,H}^{D}(c_P+zH)
 =\kappa_n(1-4z+3z^2)+\gamma H z(1-z)^2.
\]
At \(z=1/3\) the jump term is zero and the second term is
\(4\gamma H/27\).  Since \(H/\kappa_n\to\infty\) for every
\(s>1\), the population maximizer is separated from \(c_P\) by order
\(H\).  Taking \(n\) large enough makes both empirical scans converge
to that maximizer while \(b=o(H)\).  The fold-four \(K_1\) contrast is
then wholly on the linear right side and converges to zero, so the rule
returns \(\Theta\) with probability tending to one although
\(\rho_n/\kappa_n\to0\).  No strengthening of the sample-size signal
condition removes this deterministic bias.  The proposed restriction
to \(s=1\) is therefore necessary for the prescribed map unless the
model is strengthened by a cross-side derivative restriction, which is
not present and is not proposed here.

proposed_definition_changes.proposed:
Let \(m=\lfloor n/4\rfloor\), let
\[
 F_j=\{(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm\},\qquad j=1,2,3,4,
\]
and ignore observations with index larger than \(4m\).  If \(m=0\), set
\(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}=\Theta\).  Otherwise put \(p=0\) when \(s=1\) and
\(p=1\) when \(s>1\), and define, on \([0,1]\),
\[
 K_0(u)=1,\qquad K_1(u)=4-6u,
\]
with both kernels set to zero off \([0,1]\).  Thus
\[
 \int_0^1K_p(u)\,du=1,
 \qquad
 \int_0^1uK_1(u)\,du=0.
\]
For \(V\in\{D,Y\}\), a fold \(j\), a bandwidth \(h>0\), and a center
\(t\in[0,1]\), define the fixed-denominator boundary-kernel contrast
\[
 \widehat\Delta_{j,h}^{V}(t)
 =\frac{1}{mh}\sum_{i\in F_j}V_i
 \left\{
 K_p\!\left(\frac{X_i-t}{h}\right)
 -K_p\!\left(\frac{t-X_i}{h}\right)
 \right\}.
\]
Set
\[
 H=\left(\frac{\kappa_n}{2^{12}M}\right)^{1/s},
 \qquad
 J_H=\left\lfloor\frac{32}{H}\right\rfloor,
 \qquad
 \mathcal G_H=\left\{\frac14+\frac{jH}{64}:0\le j\le J_H\right\}.
\]
In particular, \(N_H:=|\mathcal G_H|\le1+32/H\).  On fold one let
\[
 \mathcal R_H
 =\left\{t\in\mathcal G_H:
 \widehat\Delta_{1,H}^{D}(t)
 \ge \max_{q\in\mathcal G_H}\widehat\Delta_{1,H}^{D}(q)
       -\frac{\kappa_n}{8}\right\}
\]
and let
\[
 \mathcal A_H
 =\bigcup_{t\in\mathcal R_H}[t-H,t+H]\cap[1/4,3/4].
\]
For every connected component \([a,b]\) of \(\mathcal A_H\), include
\(a,b\) and the points \(a+j/n\le b\); call the resulting finite set
\(\mathcal G_n(\mathcal A_H)\).  Define
\[
 \overline\Delta_H^D(t)
 =\frac12\left\{
 \widehat\Delta_{2,H}^{D}(t)+
 \widehat\Delta_{3,H}^{D}(t)
 \right\},
 \qquad
 \widehat c
 =\min\mathop{\rm arg\,max}_{t\in\mathcal G_n(\mathcal A_H)}
 \overline\Delta_H^D(t).
\]
The minimum supplies deterministic tie breaking.  Put
\(b=m^{-1/(2s+1)}\) and, with
\(L_\alpha=\log(32/\alpha)\), put
\[
 R_c=\frac{2^{16}L_\alpha}{m\kappa_n^2}+\frac1n
\]
and
\[
 r_n
 =8Mb^s+\frac{16\kappa_nR_c}{b}
   +16MH^{s-1}R_c
   +8\|K_p\|_\infty
       \sqrt{\frac{L_\alpha}{mb}}.
\]
If either \(R_c>H/8\) or \(r_n>\kappa_n/8\), set
\(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}=\Theta\).  If both checks pass, define on fold four
\[
 \widehat y(\widehat c)=\widehat\Delta_{4,b}^{Y}(\widehat c),
 \qquad
 \widehat d(\widehat c)=\widehat\Delta_{4,b}^{D}(\widehat c).
\]
The passing inequality \(8Mb^s\le\kappa_n/8\), together with
\(M\ge2\) and \(\kappa_n\le1/8\), ensures
\(b<1/4\), so these kernel windows lie in \([0,1]\).  If
\(\widehat d(\widehat c)<\kappa_n/2\), again set
\(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}=\Theta\).  In the remaining case define the sample
map
\[
 I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}
 =\operatorname{hull}\left\{\theta\in\Theta:
 \left|\widehat y(\widehat c)
       -\theta\widehat d(\widehat c)\right|\le2r_n\right\},
\]
where the hull of the empty set is the empty interval.  Every grid,
normalization, threshold, tie rule, fallback, and critical radius in this
display is deterministic given \((n,s,M,\kappa_n,\alpha)\), so this is a
measurable map of \((O_1,\ldots,O_n)\).
proposed_definition_changes.reason: The frozen construction described stages but did not define a measurable sample map.  The replacement fixes the folds, kernels, normalizations, grids, retention threshold, tie rule, localization radius, inversion radius, and fallbacks required by the directive.

\(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}=\Theta\).  If both checks pass, define on fold four
\[
 \widehat y(\widehat c)=\widehat\Delta_{4,b}^{Y}(\widehat c),
 \qquad
 \widehat d(\widehat c)=\widehat\Delta_{4,b}^{D}(\widehat c).
\]
The passing inequality \(8Mb^s\le\kappa_n/8\), together with
\(M\ge2\) and \(\kappa_n\le1/8\), ensures
\(b<1/4\), so these kernel windows lie in \([0,1]\).  If
\(\widehat d(\widehat c)<\kappa_n/2\), again set
\(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}=\Theta\).  In the remaining case define the sample
map
\[
 I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}
 =\operatorname{hull}\left\{\theta\in\Theta:
 \left|\widehat y(\widehat c)
       -\theta\widehat d(\widehat c)\right|\le2r_n\right\},
\]
where the hull of the empty set is the empty interval.  Every grid,
normalization, threshold, tie rule, fallback, and critical radius in this
display is deterministic given \((n,s,M,\kappa_n,\alpha)\), so this is a
measurable map of \((O_1,\ldots,O_n)\).

proposed.statement:
Suppose \(s=1\).  There are constants \(C_1,C_2<\infty\), depending
only on \(M,v,\alpha\), such that, for all sufficiently large \(n\), if
\(T_n\ge C_1\log(e/\kappa_n)\), then the sample map
\(I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}\) is uniformly honest over \(\mathcal P_n\) and
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_n}E_P[|I_n^{\mathrm{SI}}|]
 \le C_2\min\{1,\rho_n/\kappa_n\}.
\]
Consequently \(L_n(\kappa_n)\asymp
L_n^{\mathrm{known}}(\kappa_n)\) in this region, uniformly over
vanishing \(\kappa_n\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof uses the newly explicit scan map, the localization lemma, the causal ratio identity, and the displayed model properties directly.  The statement is restricted to the only smoothness face on which the prescribed scan is uniformly centered under the frozen class.

prose_updates.tldr: The paper studies fixed-\(\alpha\) expected length of connected honest intervals for fuzzy-RD LATE when both the compliance jump and its unknown cutoff become statistically weak.  The location-mixture constructions give a nonshrinking lower bound below the signal-to-entropy boundary.  At the Lipschitz endpoint \(s=1\), an explicit four-fold scan--refine--invert sample map attains the known-cutoff order once \(T_n=n\kappa_n^3\) dominates \(\log(e/\kappa_n)\).  For \(s>1\), the prescribed kernel argmax is not uniformly centered under the stated observable-smoothness class because an unrestricted cross-cutoff slope kink can dominate the shrinking level jump; the critical-window frontier and a strong-signal construction robust to that nuisance remain unresolved.

project_justification.fill: The project defines one observable reduced-form minimax class, embeds outcome-invariant latent monotone location mixtures in it, derives the finite-sample connected-length converse, and supplies a fully specified four-fold bias-aware scan--invert interval with proved oracle-order attainment at \(s=1\).  The proof also isolates an explicit in-class slope-kink obstruction to extending that particular scan to \(s>1\), thereby identifying the additional nuisance geometry that the all-smoothness critical and strong-signal constructions must handle.

sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: One-sided observable treatment and outcome regressions admit radius-\(M\), order-\(s\) H\"older extensions.  The proved \(s=1\) procedure uses deterministic four-fold splitting, fixed-denominator boundary-kernel treatment contrasts, a coarse \(H/64\)-resolution scan, an independent local mesh refinement, and fixed-center transformed-outcome inversion.

prose_updates.related_work: Noack and Rothe (2024) motivate the observable class: fuzzy-RD LATE is a ratio of one-sided reduced-form jumps, weak compliance defeats ordinary Wald inference, and bias-aware Anderson--Rubin inversion restores known-cutoff honesty under smooth observed regressions.  Porter and Yu (2015), Theorem 5, prove fixed-jump oracle substitution for treatment-effect estimation after an unknown cutoff in their sharp-design model.  Frick, Munk, and Sieling (2014) motivate the multiscale scan architecture, and Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, and Kato (2014) provide general maximal-control tools; neither source supplies this uniform localization-to-connected-length theorem.  M{\"u}ller and Song (1997) and Tuvaandorj (2020) analyze vanishing-jump or nonparametric location experiments rather than the causal connected-length target.  Armstrong and Koles{\'a}r (2018) supply the ordered-modulus and test-inversion template on convex fixed-index classes.  Madrid Padilla, Yu, Wang, and Rinaldo (2022) study aligned multivariate change channels without the monotone fuzzy-RD causal constraints.  Kowalska, van de Wiel, and van der Pas (2025 version) use a Bayesian unknown-cutoff fuzzy-RD specification rather than a frequentist honest minimax frontier.  Arai, Otsu, and Seo (2026) discuss fuzzy and unknown-discontinuity extensions separately.  The proved contribution here is the explicit Lipschitz-endpoint scan--refine--invert theorem.  For \(s>1\), the frozen class permits a cross-cutoff derivative kink large enough to displace the prescribed kernel-contrast maximizer, so neither fixed-jump oracle substitution nor known-cutoff Anderson--Rubin inversion closes that case.
prose_updates.interpretation: At \(s=1\), localization information \(n\kappa_n^3\) pays once for the unknown cutoff; after localization, independent fixed-center inversion has the same \(n^{-1/3}/\kappa_n\) length as if the cutoff were supplied.  The higher-smoothness obstruction is deterministic rather than a missing concentration constant: separate smooth extensions on the two sides do not control their derivative mismatch, and that mismatch can move the scan's population peak by order \(H\).
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The strong-signal theorem is proved only at \(s=1\).  For every \(s>1\), a legal linear-slope witness makes the specified \(K_1\) population contrast peak away from the true cutoff because \(H/\kappa_n\to\infty\).  No larger sample-size constant repairs that population bias.  A full \(s>1\) upper bound must use a slope-robust cutoff criterion under the same class, not import latent-cell smoothness or cross-side derivative compatibility.  The sharp fixed-\(\alpha\) critical-window law remains open for every \(s\).
prose_updates.honest_scope: The Wald interpretation, location-mixture barriers, and known-cutoff benchmark retain their stated scope over the full class.  The explicit strong-signal oracle-attainment result is uniform over the Lipschitz face \(s=1\), allows \(\kappa_n\to0\), and concerns honest connected expected length.  It is not asserted for \(s>1\): the class controls the two one-sided observable extensions separately but does not control their derivative mismatch.  No cross-side derivative condition, latent-cell H\"older condition, covariance eigenvalue floor, adaptation claim, disconnected-set claim, or Bayesian calibration claim is added.  The all-\(s\) critical-window expression and an attaining interval remain the paper's open frontier question.

statement_notes.justification: This theorem now supplies a completely evaluable honest procedure and oracle expected-length guarantee at the Lipschitz endpoint, with all grids, thresholds, fallbacks, and constants displayed.
statement_notes.gap: Known-cutoff weak-first-stage inference and fixed-jump unknown-cutoff oracle substitution do not imply uniform honest connected-length attainment when the jump vanishes.  The theorem closes that gap for \(s=1\); a slope-kink witness shows why the prescribed scan cannot close it for \(s>1\) under the same class.
statement_notes.consumer: For Lipschitz reduced forms, researchers can implement the four-fold rule and recover the known-cutoff length whenever \(n\kappa_n^3\) exceeds the logarithmic location-search cost.
